html:
The map's label for the peoples of the eastern woodlands of North America, shown from 1500 BCE to 200 BCE and again from 500 to 1400, with a gap where the map shows the Hopewell culture instead. The label undersells the region: people here began farming on their own.

The old way of life drew on deer, turkey, fish, shellfish and nuts such as hickory and acorns. Shell heaps along the rivers show how long people came back to the same places.

  • Plants: by about 2000 BCE people had domesticated squash, sunflower and seed plants such as goosefoot, the Eastern Agricultural Complex. This makes the region one of the few places in the world where farming started independently.
  • Mounds: the earthworks of Poverty Point were built between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, then the burial mounds of the Adena culture and the wide trade network of the Hopewell, which moved copper, shells and obsidian across the continent.
  • Maize: after about 800 CE maize became the main crop, and the Mississippian towns such as Cahokia rose. In the north-east, peoples grew maize, beans and squash together, the Three Sisters.

The areas still marked with this label were mostly in the north, where foraging remained the main way of life.
